findings.title: Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request
findings.body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Update line 135, Delete line 110, DeleteCollection line 163). When the handler returns, the apiserver cancels that request context, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never extends past the parent, so the legacy "safety" write is aborted (or races the cancel) instead of running to completion. Mode 3 will report success for unified storage while the legacy copy is systematically dropped, and a later rollback to legacy will be missing creates, updates, and deletes.

findings.title: Async legacy Create races on the caller's object
findings.body: After Storage.Create returns, the handler encodes the returned object while a goroutine calls Legacy.Create on the same obj pointer (line 55) with no deep copy. Storage and legacy implementations mutate metadata in place (resourceVersion, UID, timestamps). That is a data race with response serialization and can tear or overwrite the object returned to the client. Previously the legacy create finished before Create returned, so this race did not exist. Copy the object (and do not share it with the caller) before the goroutine.

findings.title: Legacy Update reapplies objInfo instead of the stored result
findings.body: Update now passes the original objInfo into asynchronous Legacy.Update (line 139). The previous implementation snapshotted the object already written to unified storage and passed an updateWrapper so legacy stored that same object. UpdatedObjectInfo is not guaranteed to be reusable or to return an independent object: a second UpdatedObject call can conflict because the request resourceVersion is the unified-storage version, not the legacy one, can apply a patch to a different base and diverge, or can return the same pointer the API response is still encoding while legacy mutates it. Legacy will not reliably receive the write that unified storage just acknowledged.

findings.title: Storage failures and legacy writes recorded on the wrong metric
findings.body: On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) with the storage start time, and Update does the same at line 129. Those paths never called legacy, so legacy failure rate is inflated and the unified-storage failure is invisible to the storage metric. DeleteCollection's async legacy path does the opposite: line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for the legacy DeleteCollection result, so legacy errors are counted as storage errors and legacy latency is not recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will point at the wrong store.

findings.title: Successful Delete uses object name as the metric kind label
findings.body: The success path of Delete calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the kind argument (line 106). Every other call, including the error path two lines above, passes options.Kind. Object names are unbounded, so each deleted object creates a new Prometheus series on that label and the process (and any scraper) will grow memory without bound under normal delete traffic.

findings.title: Legacy write failures are no longer logged
findings.body: The async legacy Create (line 56), Update (line 140), Delete (line 113), and DeleteCollection (line 165) ignore the error except for a duration metric. The previous synchronous implementation logged these failures. Combined with the mis-labeled metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves the two stores diverged with no log line an operator can alert on. The request still returns success, which is intended, but the safety write's failure must be logged.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
findings.body: Each successful write spawns an unbounded goroutine that may block on legacy storage for up to 10s, and nothing tracks those goroutines. Destroy (line 172) immediately calls Legacy.Destroy() and Storage.Destroy(). On shutdown or storage teardown, in-flight legacy creates/updates/deletes run against a closed store (panic or error) or are dropped when the process exits, so the safety copy is lost exactly when it is needed for rollback.

findings.title: Delete puts the unscoped logger into the context
findings.body: Delete builds log with name, kind, and method, then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of klog.NewContext(ctx, log). Storage.Delete and the async Legacy.Delete therefore do not see those fields, unlike Create, Update, and DeleteCollection, which install the enriched logger. Delete failures will be missing the object identity in contextual logs.

findings.title: Tests never wait for or assert the async legacy write
findings.body: Mode 3 unit tests return as soon as the synchronous storage call finishes (Create at line 65, and the same pattern in Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection). They never wait for the goroutine, never AssertExpectations, and would still pass if the legacy write were removed. The success-path mocks are also invoked from a goroutine after the test can return, which races testify's mock. The new playlist integration cases (pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go line 132 and the unified-storage mode 3 case) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares the legacy HTTP API (line 529 and getFromBothAPIs) with k8s results. That assumed synchronous dual-write; under mode 3 it will flake or fail when the legacy copy has not landed yet.
